script.title: Why IKEA Is Losing Thousands of Crores in India

segments.text: IKEA sells thousands of desks every single day across India. Yet, they just pushed their Indian profit goal all the way to 2029.
segments.broll: close up hands holding allen wrench screw

segments.text: Think about it, yaar. You walk into their massive blue stores for cheap furniture, end up spending five thousand rupees on candles and meatballs, and leave happy.
segments.broll: wide shot busy shopping mall store entrance

segments.text: But behind those glowing yellow signs lies a massive cash burn. Today, we decode why the world's biggest furniture giant is losing money in India, and why your local carpenter might be beating them at their own game.
segments.broll: aerial shot highway leading to big store

segments.text: Now, to understand IKEA's pain, you have to look at how Western shoppers buy furniture versus how Indians do.
segments.broll: close up wood carpenter cutting timber

segments.text: In Europe, labor is expensive. Assembling your own bed saves you hundreds of Euros. It is called the Do-It-Yourself model.
segments.broll: medium shot man reading instruction manual box

segments.text: But in India? DIY was a massive cultural shock. Why spend four hours sweating over a thousand tiny screws when your local carpenter, your trusted mistri ji, builds custom teak wood furniture delivered straight to your bedroom?
segments.broll: close up carpenter hammering nail wood

segments.text: IKEA quickly realized that Indian customers flatly refused to assemble tables themselves. So, they had to hire third-party assembly services like Urban Company, instantly slicing off a chunk of their profit margin.
segments.broll: medium shot delivery person holding tools

segments.text: But assembly was just the first hurdle; the real nightmare was Indian real estate.
segments.broll: aerial shot city skyscrapers construction site

segments.text: IKEA doesn't open small shops. They build gigantic box stores spanning over four hundred thousand square feet. That is roughly the size of seven football fields!
segments.broll: wide shot massive warehouse building sunny day

segments.text: Buying five to ten acres of land inside cities like Mumbai or Bengaluru costs thousands of crores. So, IKEA built their stores on the outer fringes of the city, twenty-five kilometers away from main residential hubs.
segments.broll: aerial view long highway traffic evening

segments.text: For an average Indian family, buying a ₹2,000 coffee table meant spending three hours in city traffic and paying ₹500 in cab fares. The sheer friction of getting there turned weekly buyers into once-a-year weekend tourists.
segments.broll: slow motion city traffic congestion evening

segments.text: If getting shoppers into stores was tough, getting furniture into the country was an even bigger puzzle.
segments.broll: wide shot cargo ship ocean containers

segments.text: Indian regulations require single-brand retail foreign companies to source thirty percent of their goods locally within five years.
segments.broll: close up textile worker machine factory

segments.text: Sourcing high-quality solid wood at scale inside India proved tough. Import duties on foreign furniture hit twenty percent, driving up landed costs and squeezing profits even further.
segments.broll: medium shot inspector holding clipboard factory

segments.text: To keep footfalls high, IKEA relied heavily on their famous food courts, selling ₹200 chicken meatballs and vegetable biryani. But while food brings crowds, you cannot sustain a multi-billion dollar retail footprint selling ₹50 coffee mugs and ₹150 plates of biryani.
segments.broll: close up plate hot food restaurant desk

segments.text: If you are enjoying this deep dive into Indian business strategies, smash that subscribe button right now to help Paisa Decoded reach more curious minds.
segments.broll: close up hand pressing red button screen

segments.text: Facing continuous EBITDA losses, IKEA realized their global playbook was failing in India.
segments.broll: medium shot business meeting discussion room

segments.text: So, they kicked off a complete transformation. Instead of relying solely on giant outer-city megastores, IKEA started opening small-format stores right inside city shopping malls in places like Mumbai.
segments.broll: wide shot modern shopping mall interior escalator

segments.text: They also expanded aggressively into e-commerce, opening online delivery across major metro cities so you can buy a sofa without driving two hours through city traffic.
segments.broll: close up smartphone screen browsing shopping app
broll_alt: hand typing mobile phone store app

segments.text: Pushing their profitability goal to FY29 isn't a sign of failure—it is a long-term play. India's home decor market is projected to reach over thirty billion dollars, and IKEA is betting big that online delivery plus smaller city stores will finally turn their red ink into solid profit.
segments.broll: aerial shot modern city cityscape skyline sunrise

script.description:
IKEA is the biggest furniture brand on earth, but why is it burning cash in India? In this video, we break down the economics of IKEA India, from their high real estate costs to the cultural mismatch of the DIY model.

You'll learn why Indian shoppers prefer local carpenters, how 30% local sourcing rules affect retail pricing, and why IKEA had to pivot from giant outer-city stores to small city mall outlets and e-commerce.

Subscribe to Paisa Decoded for actionable breakdowns of Indian business models, brand strategies, and practical money concepts every week!
